Chapter 7: The Masks We Wear—Identity, Gender, and the Role of the Other.
Every morning, when you step out into the world, there’s this quiet choice you make—deciding which face you’ll show. Now, in Mexico, the idea of the mask isn’t just a figure of speech. It’s woven into daily life. It’s how people navigate a space that can feel both close and, at times, unwelcoming.
The mask? It’s protection. But here’s the thing—it can also turn into a prison. You start wondering, where does the mask end... and where does the real you begin?
Imagine a young woman walking through a busy market. She’s carrying the weight of expectations. Sure, she moves with confidence and keeps her head up, but she’s learned the rules—how to speak, how to dress, how to avoid drawing the wrong kind of attention.
For her, the mask is both a shield and a disguise. It helps her fit in. It keeps her safe, but it also hides a part of who she really is.
Now, for men, the mask can look pretty different. There’s this constant pressure to be strong, to never let vulnerability show, to prove yourself in a world that seems to reward toughness above all else.
Whether it’s the laughter between friends, or the rituals of work and play, there’s an invisible code—a way of acting that leaves very little space for doubt or weakness.
But these masks go beyond just gender. They’re also about being the other—the outsider, the stranger. In a country shaped by conquest and colonization, questions of who truly belongs are never far away.
So, the mask becomes a tool for handling difference, for drawing lines between yourself and everyone else.
Picture a family dinner, where talk turns to a neighbor who’s just “not quite like us.” There’s this mix of curiosity and unease—a little bit of fascination, but also a thread of fear. The mask lets people interact without giving too much away, helping everyone keep a sense of order in a world that can feel unpredictable.
Still, underneath it all, there’s this deep longing. A wish to be seen, to be understood, to connect—without the masks. And in those rare moments of true closeness, when the mask finally slips, there’s a wave of relief, but also a jolt of vulnerability.
It’s a powerful reminder that searching for our identity is always a balancing act—a dance between needing protection and wanting to truly connect.
Over time, you start to see that these masks are both helpful and limiting. They keep us safe, but they also keep us apart.
So, the real challenge? Finding ways to let those masks fall, taking the risk of being seen, and creating spaces where your true self can finally step forward.
